title: Enhanced efficiency for carbon dioxide electroreduction to formate by electrodeposition Sn on Cu nanowires
abstract: Electroreduction of CO2 to formate is one of the most promising methods for CO2 utilization and conversion. However, low conversion efficiency and poor stability of electrodes limit its practical application. In this study, Sn are electrodeposited on copper nanowires (Sn/Nano-Cu) to serve as the electrode for the electroreduction of CO2 to formate. Results show that Sn nanoparticles are uniformly distributed on copper nanowires. When the potential of − 1.2 V (vs. RHE) is applied, the prepared Sn/Nano-Cu electrode exhibits the maximum Faradaic efficiency as high as 86.8 % with a current density of 38.0 mA cm 2. The formate production rate reaches 575.1 ± 24 μmol h-1 cm 2, which is 1.9 and 2.9 times that of the Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrode, respectively. The excellent CO2 electrochemical reduction performance may be attributed to the large electroactive surface area and low charge transfer resistance. Moreover, the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode can maintain high Faraday efficiency during 25 h test. The superior electrocatalytic performance as well as good stability for CO2 electroreduction is achieved by the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode.

Enhanced efficiency for carbon dioxide electroreduction to formate by electrodeposition Sn on Cu nanowires
Guoqian Chen a,b, Dingding Ye a,b,*, Rong Chen a,b, Jun Li a,b, Xun Zhu a,b, Qiang Liao a,b

Keywords: Electroreduction Carbon dioxide Tin Copper nanowire Formate
A B S T R A C T
Electroreduction of CO2 to formate is one of the most promising methods for CO2 utilization and conversion. However, low conversion efficiency and poor stability of electrodes limit its practical application. In this study, Sn are electrodeposited on copper nanowires (Sn/Nano-Cu) to serve as the electrode for the electroreduction of CO2 to formate. Results show that Sn nanoparticles are uniformly distributed on copper nanowires. When the potential of − 1.2 V (vs. RHE) is applied, the prepared Sn/Nano-Cu electrode exhibits the maximum Faradaic efficiency as high as 86.8 % with a current density of 38.0 mA cm− 2. The formate production rate reaches 575.1 ± 24 μmol h-1 cm− 2, which is 1.9 and 2.9 times that of the Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrode, respectively. The excellent CO2 electrochemical reduction performance may be attributed to the large electroactive surface area and low charge transfer resistance. Moreover, the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode can maintain high Faraday efficiency during 25 h test. The superior electrocatalytic performance as well as good stability for CO2 electroreduction is achieved by the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration in global atmosphere has risen from the pre-industrial value of 278 ppm to 405 ppm by 2017 resulting from the excessive use of fossil fuels [1,2]. The large increase in the concentration of CO2 leads to the greenhouse effect and further the climate change issue. Therefore, there is no doubt that effective measures must be carried out to reduce the content of CO2 in the atmosphere. In recent years, the concept of CO2 utilization and conversion has attracted much attention of researchers. Converting CO2 into hydrocarbon fuels by catalytic hydrogenation reduction [3,4] bioelectrochemical [5,6], photochemical [7,8] and electrochemical methods [9–11] has been explored. In particular, electroreduction of CO2 to useful chemicals is considered as a promising technology for CO2 conversion because of its mild operation conditions as well as providing a green and convenient way to store the intermittent renewable electricity.
Since formic acid is a widely used material in industries and also a promising fuel for fuel cells, formic acid or formate production by electroreduction of CO2 has drawn increasing attention. A number of heterogeneous catalysts (such as In, Pb, Sn, etc) have been developed for
formic acid or formate production [12,13]. Among them, the Sn electrode is considered to have sufficient potential as a catalyst because of its low cost, high hydrogen evolution potential and good selectivity for formic acid [14,15]. It is found that the electrocatalytic activity of Sn electrodes is highly correlated with structure and morphology of catalysts [16]. Machunda et al. [17] electrodeposited Sn catalyst on carbon paper for electrochemical CO2 reduction and yielded a Faradaic efficiency of only 18 % for formate. Fu et al. [18] reported a novel hierarchical SnO2 microsphere catalyst for electrochemical CO2 reduction. At –1.7 V (vs. SHE), a Faradaic efficiency of 62 % was obtained. Won et al. [19] demonstrated a significantly increased Faradaic efficiency for formate by heat-treated Sn dendrite electrodes compared with the Sn foil electrodes. They proved that the initial oxygen content on the electrode surface was strongly related to formate selectivity. Besides, the effect of the SnOx layer on electroreduction of CO2 into formic acid/formate have been studied [20–22]. Zhao and Wang [23] electrodeposited Sn catalysts on copper substrate and found that catalytic performance is influenced by microstructure and thickness of Sn electrode. The Faradaic efficiency reached 91 % at potential of –1.4 V (vs. SCE), but the current density was only 0.9–1.4 mA cm− 2. Wang et al. [24] fabricated the Sn/f-Cu electrode via electrodeposition Sn on copper foam and the highest Faradaic

They also fabricated porous Sn-based film on copper foil by electrodeposition and proved that Faradaic efficiency is affected by the deposition time, the electrolysis potential as well as the Sn-based film thickness [25]. The electrodes with nano-structures are employed in electrochemical reduction CO2 for formate due to large surface area. Du et al. [26] synthesized the nanoporous tin foam electrode by electrodeposition on a tin substrate, showing a good selectivity as well as fast production rate into formate. High Faradaic efficiency of 90 % for formate with current density above 23 mA cm− 2 was yielded. Although several studies about CO2 electroreduction to formate with Sn-based electrodes have been conducted, electrodeposition Sn on nanowire structure has not been reported. Since it is difficult to synthesize Sn nanowires directly [27,28], developing Sn electrode coated on nanowire structure is expected to possess good electrocatalytic performance for CO2 electroreduction.
Herein, Sn was electrodeposited on Cu nanowires (Sn/Nano-Cu) as the electrode for formate production by CO2 electroreduction. A Cu foil loading Sn (Sn/Cu) electrode and a commercial Sn foil electrode were used to compare. Sn nanoparticles were successfully coated and welldistributed on the surface of Cu nanowires. Electrochemical measurements showed that the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 86.8 % with current density of 38.0 mA cm− 2 under − 1.2 V (vs. RHE). Moreover, excellent electrocatalytic performance and superior stability of the prepared Sn/Nano-Cu electrode were demonstrated.

sections.heading: 2.1. Electrode preparation
sections.text:
Copper nanowires were synthesized on a Cu foil by the oxidationreduction method reported before [29], as shown in Fig. 1. The Cu foil (1 cm2) (0.1 mm in thickness) was cleaned by the following procedure, i. e.: (i) washing in 3 M HCl ultrasonically to remove oxides on the surface, (ii) rinsing with deionized (DI) water, (iii) cleaning in the mixed solution of ethanol and acetone (1:1 in volume ratio) ultrasonically to remove organic impurities; (iv) rinsing with DI water and drying in the air. The pretreated Cu foil was placed in the reaction solution (0.1 M NH4SO3 in 2.5 M NaOH) for 30 min, after that the surface of the Cu foil turned to blue. Then the sample was washed by DI water and dried in the air. To synthesize Cu nanowires, the sample was further immersed in 50 mL of 0.5 M NaBH4 with stirring for about 2 h, rinsed by DI water and dried in a vacuum oven. Finally, the Cu(OH)2 was reduced to Cu and the surface of sample changed to puce. Cu nanowires were successfully synthesized on both sides of Cu foil.
Sn catalyst was coated on the surface of copper nanowires by the electrodeposition method. The electroplating solution was prepared as the previous study [25]. 0.05 M sodium citrate solution was prepared at first, then the pH value was adjusted to about 6.0 with H2SO4. SnCl2 was dissolved in the above solution to form the electroplating solution with a concentration of 0.018 M, which was stirred at least 10 h before the electrodeposition. With a Pt foil (4 cm2) counter electrode, Sn catalyst was electrodeposited on the surface of copper nanowires by applying a constant current density (3 mA cm− 2) for 15 min. The obtained sample was denoted as Sn/Nano-Cu. In addition, a Sn/Cu electrode as well as a commercial Sn foil electrode was employed as contrast samples. The
same electrodeposition process was performed directly on the Cu foil to prepare the Sn/Cu electrode. The Sn foil was only cleaned in ethanol, acetone and DI water in turn.

sections.heading: 2.2. Physical characterization
sections.text: Physical characterizations including XPS, XRD, SEM, EDS were conducted on the prepared electrodes. The morphology of electrodes was detected using the scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi, SU8010) at 10 kV acceleration voltage combined with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). X-ray diffraction (XRD, BRUKER D8 ADVANCE) was used to character the composition of electrodes. In addition, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific, ESCALAB 250Xi) spectra were obtained with a Al-Kα (hv = 1486.6 eV) X-ray source at a power of 150 W.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrochemical characterization
sections.text:
All electrochemical measurements were carried out by an electrochemical workstation (Bio-Logic, VMP3). A Pt foil (4 cm2) and Ag/AgCl electrode were employed as the counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively. The Sn/Nano-Cu, Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrodes acted as working electrodes (1 cm2) and the electrolyte was 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. All experiments were performed in a temperature-controlled room (30 ± 2 ◦C).
Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was tested in N2 or CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution with 20 mV s− 1 scan rate. Electroactive surface area (ESA) was assessed by the double layer capacitance of electrode (Cdl) [30], which was estimated by cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurement in N2-saturated KHCO3 solution over the potential range from 0.05 to 0.25 V (vs. RHE). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test was performed over a frequency range from 100 KHz to 10 mHz with an amplitude of 30 mV at − 0.6 V vs. RHE. All potentials in results were standardized to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE).

sections.heading: 2.4. Product analysis
sections.text:
CO2 reduction experiments were performed at different potentials for 1 h in a conventional H-type cell (with electrolyte volume of 110 mL in each chamber) separated by Nafion 212 membrane. The CO2 gas flow rate was 30 mL min− 1. The amount of produced formate was quantitatively analyzed using an ion chromatograph (ICS-5000, Themo Scientific) and the calibration curve for formate concentration is shown in Fig. S1. In the experiment, the tested solution is diluted 20 times to detect the formate concentration. According to the peak area obtained by ion chromatograph and the calibration curve, we can calculate the detected formate concentration, then multiply the diluted times 20 and the electrolyte volume (110 mL), divided by the reduction time (1 h) and the electrode area (1 cm2), finally obtain the production rate (μmol h− 1 cm− 2). If the formate concentration is very low, the diluted times could be reduced to 10 to make sure the tested value within the detect limit. In addition, only formate production was considered the in the experiment,

sections.heading: 3.1. Characterizations of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode
sections.text:
The morphologies of the prepared electrodes were characterized by SEM. Micrographs of Cu nanowires on Cu foil are shown in Fig. 2(a)–(c). Nanowires are successfully synthesized and distributed uniformly on the Cu foil. As shown in Fig. 2(c), the width of a single nanowire is about 200 nm. Moreover, the rich pore structure and rough surface can be observed, which could provide large specific surface areas for the further Sn loading. XRD was conducted to confirm the synthesized nanowires as Cu, as shown in Fig. 2(d). It is found that for both the Cu foil and nanowires, the diffraction peaks at 2θ of 43.4◦, 50.6◦ and 74.2◦ correspond to the (111), (200) and (220) facets of Cu crystal (PDF#04-0836), respectively. This indicates that Cu(OH)2 is completely reduced to Cu and Cu nanowires are successfully synthesized through reduction in NaBH4 aqueous solution.
Micrographs of the Sn/Nano-Cu and Sn/Cu electrodes are shown in Fig. 3. For the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode, a few aggregation substances are found around Cu nanowires, which may result from Sn aggregation during the electrodeposition process. The morphology of the Sn/NanoCu electrode is similar with that before electrodeposition (Fig. 2b and c). To prove that Sn nanoparticles were electrodeposited on surface of Cu nanowires, EDS surface scanning was conducted and the result was shown in Fig. S2. It is demonstrated that Sn nanoparticles are welldistributed on surface of Cu nanowires. However, for the Sn/Cu electrode, a porous film is formed on surface of Cu foil, but less pore spaces are observed compared with the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode.
XRD patterns of the Sn/Nano-Cu, Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrodes are presented in Fig. 4. Only diffraction peaks of Sn can be observed for the Sn foil electrode. However, for both the Sn/Nano-Cu and Sn/Cu electrodes, main peaks corresponded to (200), (220) and (211) facets of the electrodeposited Sn (PDF#04-0673) can be seen besides the diffraction peaks of Cu. This confirms that Sn nanoparticles are successfully
electrodeposited on surface of Cu foil or Cu nanowires. XPS analysis was conducted to confirm the surface chemical states of the Sn/Nano-Cu and Sn/Cu electrodes. Fig. 5(a) shows the highresolution Sn 3d XPS spectra of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode. Obviously, two Sn species peaks appear on the surface of the electrode. The peaks at binding energies of 495.02 and 486.6 eV correspond to the 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 peaks of SnOx. Moreover, other two peaks at binding energies of 493.19 and 484.77 eV can be attributed to the 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 peaks of Sn◦. This is consistent with the results in the previous study [31]. In addition, XPS fitting results indicate that the peak area ratios of SnOx and Sn◦ are 84 % and 16 %, respectively. Fig. 5(b) presents the high-resolution Sn 3d XPS spectra of the Sn/Cu electrode. Two peaks at 494.64 and 486.24 eV can be attributed to SnOx, which shows a slight shift to lower energy compared to the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode. The other two peaks at 492.84 and 484.42 eV correspond to the 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 peaks of Sn◦. The peak area ratios of SnOx and Sn◦ are 60 % and 40 %, respectively. Therefore, the result demonstrates that more tin oxide exists on the surface of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode. The reason is mainly ascribed to the fact that more tin is oxidized to SnOx owing to the larger specific surface area of Cu nanowires.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The ESA can be evaluated by the double layer capacitance of the Sn/ Nano-Cu, Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrodes, which are calculated based on CV curves at different scan rates (Fig. S3). The result is shown in Fig. 6 (a), in which the slope of the line represents the double layer capacitance of the tested electrode. The double layer capacitances are 0.0059 F cm− 2, 0.0019 F cm− 2, 0.00014 F cm− 2 for the Sn/Nano-Cu, Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrodes, respectively. Therefore, the ESA for the Sn/ Nano-Cu electrode is estimated to be roughly 3.1 and 42 times as high as that of the Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrode, respectively. The larger ESA may mainly ascribe to the rich pore structure of the prepared Sn/Nano-Cu electrode (Fig. 3(a)). The measured double layer capacitance may be due to different species on the surface. This result suggests the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode may provide more active sites for the electroreduction of CO2. To further understand the kinetic performance of three electrodes,

Tafel plots were obtained and presented in Fig. 6(b). Tafel slopes of the Sn/Nano-Cu, Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrode are 174, 206 and 135 mV dec1, respectively. The Tafel slope of Sn foil electrode is similar with that in
literature (134 mV dec-1) [19], which is lower than that of Sn/Nano-Cu electrode. This may be attributed to different substrate materials and surface structures for these two electrodes. However, compared with Sn/Cu electrode, Sn/Nano-Cu electrode shows a smaller Tafel slope, suggesting its certain advantageous for electrochemical CO2 reduction.
EIS measurements were performed to study the electrical conductivity and the kinetics of electron-transfer processes of the three electrodes. Fig. 6(c) presents Nyquist impedance plots obtained for the above three electrodes at − 0.6 V (vs. RHE). It can be seen that the ohmic resistances mainly caused by the electrolyte solution were almost constant for three electrodes. It is noted that the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode shows smaller impedance arcs than other two electrodes, which suggests it exhibits the lower interfacial charge-transfer resistance, and hence ensures faster electron transfer. Therefore, it is expected that faster electrochemical reduction occurs on the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode.

sections.heading: 3.3. Electroreduction of CO2 to formate
sections.text:
Electroreduction of CO2 by three electrodes was evaluated in 0.1 M KHCO3 solutions. Fig. 7(a) illustrates linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) with three electrodes in N2- or CO2-bubbled electrolyte. Obviously, for Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrodes, little difference is found between the

current density in the CO2-bubbled and N2-bubbled electrolyte. However, Sn/Nano-Cu electrode shows larger current densities in the CO2bubbled electrolyte than those in the N2-bubbled one. This indicates that the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode shows excellent electrocatalytic activities for CO2 reduction. More importantly, although the Sn/Nano-Cu and Sn/Cu electrodes exhibit the same current density in the atmosphere of N2, the current density of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode is evidently higher than that of the Sn/Cu electrode in the atmosphere of CO2. In addition, the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode shows a much more positive onset potential compared with the other two electrodes. This demonstrates the prepared Sn/Nano-Cu electrode shows higher electrocatalytic activity for electrochemical reduction of CO2.
Fig. 7(b) illustrates Faradaic efficiencies for formate generation evaluated at various applied potentials for three electrodes. One can clearly observe that the Faradaic efficiency for formate goes up at first until − 1.2 V for all three electrodes. Then, as the applied potential becomes more negative, the Faradaic efficiency decreases due to production of other products. As a result, the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode reaches the highest Faradaic efficiency of 86.8 % at − 1.2 V (vs. RHE), which is about 1.2 and 1.3 times that of Sn/Cu electrode (72 %) and Sn foil electrode (66.8 %). Moreover, the Faradaic efficiency for formate is comparable with other similar studies (Table 1). Fig. 7(c) illustrates current densities at different applied potentials for three electrodes. As the applied potential increases, the current density increases for all electrodes. The Sn/ Nano-Cu electrode exhibits larger current density than the other two electrodes due to its superior electrochemical performance. Specifically, current density curves of three electrodes at − 1.2 V (vs. RHE) and the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode at different potentials are presented in Figs. S4 and S5, respectively. The fluctuation of the curve suggests that bubbles are generated because of the hydrogen evolution reaction. The current density for the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode is 38.0 mA cm− 2, which is 71 % and 127 % higher than that for Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrode, respectively. This is in accordance with the LSV results displayed in Fig. 7(a).
Production rates for formate of the Sn/Nano-Cu, Sn/Cu and Sn foil
electrodes are also tested at different applied potentials as illustrated in Fig. 7(d). The formate production rates of three electrodes increase as the potential decreases. The formate production rate of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode shows a distinct advantage over the other two electrodes. At − 1.2 V (vs. RHE), the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode yields a formate production rate of 575.1 ± 24 μmol h− 1 cm− 2, which is 1.9 and 2.9 times the value of the Sn/Cu electrode (298.3 ± 36.4 μmol h− 1 cm− 2) and the Sn foil electrode (198.9 ± 13.8 μmol h− 1 cm− 2). This may be attributed to the larger specific surface area and higher electrocatalytic activity of the Sn/ Nano-Cu electrode with nanowire structure.

sections.heading: 3.4. Stability of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode
sections.text: Stability is also significant for electrodes in practical applications. Constant potential (− 1.2 V vs. RHE) was employed to investigate the stability in a flowing CO2-bubbled 0.1 M KHCO3 solution under 2 mL min− 1 flow rate. The corresponding current density and Faradaic efficiency during 25 h are illustrated in Fig. 8. A slight decrease in the current density can be seen before 7 h, and then it maintains a stable value of 43 mA cm-2. This is may be the activation process of the electrode. The Faradaic efficiency at 2 h reaches 87 %, then drops slightly, and remains a stable value of 70 %. The decreased Faradaic efficiency may be ascribed to the catalyst shedding and particle agglomeration during the long time electrolysis. This indicates that the prepared Sn/ Nano-Cu electrode shows a superior stability for electrochemical reduction of CO2.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this study, the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode for electroreduction of CO2 was prepared by electrodepositing Sn catalyst on Cu nanowires, which was fabricated by oxidation-reduction method on the Cu foil. The results of SEM, EDS and XRD indicated that Sn nanoparticles were coated on copper nanowires successively. Compared with the Sn/Cu and Sn foil electrodes, the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode possessed a lower interfacial charge-transfer resistance and a larger ESA. As a result, the current density of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode for electroreduction of CO2 reached 38.0 mA cm− 2, which was significantly larger than that of the other two electrodes. Moreover, the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode displayed a Faradaic efficiency of 86.8 % for producing formate at − 1.2 V (vs. RHE). Moreover, the formate production rate of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode reaches 575.1 ± 24 μmol h-1 cm− 2, which is the highest among three electrodes. Electrochemical stability of the Sn/Nano-Cu electrode was confirmed by electrolysis at − 1.2 V (vs. RHE) during the long period of 25 h. In a word, the prepared Sn/Nano-Cu electrode with excellent performance shows great prospects for electroreduction of CO2.
